passage: Leela, listen. You say your online friend is perfect, and I smile, because I was twenty once. I am Chetan, and I wrote letters for a year to a girl in Nagpur named Sumitra. Every letter was poems, jokes, the best of her week. I built a whole person out of paper. When I finally took the train, she was late, she laughed loudly with her mouth full, and she did not like my favourite songs. That first evening I nearly went home, thinking she was not the girl in the letters. But her mother handed us a bowl of peas to shell, and over that bowl I saw it: the letters were her good afternoons, and this was her whole day. I stayed a week. We walked to the vegetable market and argued about songs. Meet yours over something ordinary, beta, not only on a screen.

qa.q: How did Chetan travel to meet Sumitra?
How did Chetan feel that first evening, and why did Chetan nearly go home?
qa.a: Chetan felt disappointed, because Sumitra was late, laughed loudly with her mouth full and did not like Chetan's songs, so she did not match the person built out of the letters.

qa.q: What advice does Chetan's story give Leela?
qa.a: Meet the online friend in an ordinary setting, expect the real person to differ from the highlights, and do not drop them at the first flaw.

qa.q: What would have changed if Chetan had gone home that evening?
qa.a: He would have left the real Sumitra for a paper image, and never learned who she was over the week of walks and arguments about songs.

grounding: An elder recalls a long-distance crush who seemed perfect from letters, and how meeting in ordinary settings showed the real person.
